stages.name: Command economy problems and the mixed economy
stages.title: Command economy problems and the mixed economy
stages.sub: Why planners struggle to know what to produce, and how mixed economies respond to the failings of both command and free markets.

steps.q: In a market, if trainers become scarce, their price rises and tells factories to make more. In a command economy, the state sets production targets instead of prices. What has the state lost, that normally carries this information?
steps.right: The price signal showing what is scarce
steps.wrong: The factory that makes the trainers
steps.hint: In a market, what normally moves first when something becomes scarce?

steps.q: A central planner has to set output targets for millions of different goods, from bread to trainers, across the whole country, without prices to guide them. Can one planning body realistically know exactly how much of everything people want?
steps.right: No, it cannot know this in detail
steps.wrong: Yes, if it collects enough data
steps.hint: Think about the sheer number of goods and the millions of individual preferences behind each one.

steps.q: Without prices to signal scarcity, and without full knowledge of what everyone wants, what is likely to happen to the planner's output decisions?
steps.right: They miscalculate and produce the wrong amounts
steps.wrong: They still match supply to demand closely
steps.hint: If the planner cannot see scarcity signals and cannot know every want, how accurate can their targets be?

steps.q: A government sees that command economies plan well but miscalculate what to produce, while free markets are efficient but under-provide things like street lighting. If it wants to keep some planning and some free markets, what must it do?
steps.wrong: Pick one system and remove the other completely
steps.hint: Both pure systems have a flaw. What kind of economy keeps parts of both?
